title: A Robot That Knows How Lost It Is: Dead Reckoning, Beacon Fixes, and a Fence Buffer That Is Only as Good as the Drift It Assumes

questions.question: The wheel base is 5 percent out. What does it cost when driving straight?
options: Nothing: it only divides the difference between the wheels

questions.question: A wheel 1 percent big gave 1.66 m at 10 m. What was the error at 20 m and 30 m?
options: 6.55 and 14.49: about four and nine times, since the error goes as the square of the distance
questions.explanation: A centimetre a metre at the start is a metre at 100 m.

questions.question: Why do fixes every 2 s leave an error of 1.42 m when each fix is good to 0.1 m?
options: The error is set by the time between fixes: the drift between them, and the fix does not correct the heading, which is what is wrong
questions.explanation: Bounded by the interval, not by the fix.

questions.question: A fence on the believed position was given no buffer. What happened to the robot whose truth left the corridor after 9.6 m?
options: It never stopped: the belief stays on the axis, so the fence never trips, and the robot ended at y = -18.3 m
questions.explanation: A fence with the right polygon and the wrong position is not a fence.

questions.question: Which assumed drifts stopped the robot before the truth left the corridor?
options: 0.20 and 0.40 m per metre: 0.05 and 0.10 stopped it after the truth was outside, and the real drift at the edge was 0.156 and growing
questions.explanation: Assume the drift for the longest distance between fixes.

questions.question: What do fixes every 5 s add to the safety argument?
options: Range: with the same assumed drift the robot went 8.7 m before it had to stop, against 5.1 m without
questions.explanation: The beacon buys distance, not safety.
